vignette:
Margot

Margot was twenty-three when the stalking began. She had been teaching high school English for less than a year, still finding her rhythm in the classroom, when a parent started appearing outside the school building at dismissal. At first it seemed like coincidence-a man in his fifties, always at the edge of the parking lot, always watching. Then he began waiting near her car. She changed her route home. He found the new route. Within weeks, he knew her schedule better than she did: which coffee shop she visited on Tuesday mornings, which grocery store she preferred, the gym where she went three times a week. The police came, took a report, told her to document everything. Nothing changed. The man would appear and disappear like a phantom, sometimes leaving notes on her windshield-not threatening exactly, but intimate in a way that made her skin crawl. I know where you are. I see you. By the time a restraining order was finally issued, six months had passed. He was arrested once, released, and the fear didn't end-it simply transformed into something more diffuse and corrosive.

That was five years ago. Margot is twenty-eight now, still teaching, still in the same city, though the stalker long ago moved away or lost interest. But something in her remained frozen in that period of being hunted. The heavy breathing she sometimes hears in crowded spaces-a man standing too close on the subway, or the sound of someone's labored exhalation behind her in the hallway at school-sends her heart into her throat. These sounds are not the stalker's breathing; she knows this rationally. Yet the moment she hears them, her mind floods with the memory of his presence, the feeling of being tracked, and a terrible certainty blooms that she is being followed again, that she has somehow failed to escape, that it will never truly end.

The sound of authority-a police siren, a uniformed officer walking past-triggers something equally raw. When a campus security guard approached her in the school parking lot last month, Margot's body reacted before her mind could catch up: her chest tightened, her vision narrowed, and fragments of memory crashed through her consciousness in jagged pieces. She remembered the officer who had come to take her statement years ago, remembered the helplessness of sitting in his car while he explained there was nothing they could do yet, and in that moment of seeing the uniform, she was certain again that she was in danger, that the authorities could not protect her, that she was alone. The memory was not complete-she could not articulate why the officer's presence felt like a threat rather than a refuge-but the feeling of being followed, of being watched, surged back with such force that she had to excuse herself and sit in her car for twenty minutes.

What Margot has come to believe, across these five years, is that people cannot be trusted. The stalker had seemed ordinary, respectable even, until he wasn't. The police had seemed capable of helping, and they hadn't. Once she had internalized this conviction that danger could arrive from anywhere and that authority could not protect her, the world became a minefield of potential threats. Because she was now certain that threat could wear any face and arrive at any moment, her mind had become a filter that caught and magnified ambiguity-a man standing too close on the subway, a stranger asking directions, even the sound of breathing behind her in a hallway were no longer innocent but potential confirmations of danger. Her belief that she could not afford to misjudge anyone meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention, demanding explanation, demanding vigilance. A man standing too close on the subway, a stranger asking directions, even the sound of breathing behind her in a hallway-each of these ordinary stimuli now registered as potentially sinister, filtered through her certainty that she could not afford to misjudge anyone or anything. Colleagues at school sometimes ask her why she seems distant, why she doesn't go to after-work drinks anymore, and she cannot explain to them that she has come to believe her life has fundamentally been destroyed-not in some dramatic, obvious way, but in the slow erosion of her ability to feel safe around others. This conviction that the world is dangerous and that she must remain vigilant at all times now colors how she interprets every ambiguous social encounter. When a stranger approaches her at the grocery store to ask for directions, she feels threatened, certain that something is wrong, that this is how it begins. Her belief that she had failed to escape the first time, that she remained fundamentally unsafe despite the passage of years, meant that each new ambiguous encounter-a person in her peripheral vision, an unfamiliar car in the parking lot, the sound of footsteps matching her pace-became evidence that the threat was still active, still closing in. The conviction that it would happen again transformed ordinary moments into potential danger; she moved through her days as if they were mined, and every silence, every stranger, every unexpected sound registered first as threat before her rational mind could catch up. When her partner reaches out to touch her shoulder from behind, she sometimes flinches, her body reacting as if the threat is still active, still closing in.

The memories themselves are fragmented and unreliable. Some moments from that six-month period are vivid-the texture of the note left on her windshield, the specific shade of his jacket-while others have vanished entirely. She knows he followed her to her apartment building one evening, but she cannot access the memory of what happened after; there is only a blank space and a bone-deep sense of violation. When she tries to describe these experiences to her partner, the words scatter. She becomes frustrated, almost angry, at her inability to articulate what happened, as if the incompleteness of her account somehow proves her fear is irrational. Yet the fragments that do surface-a flash of his face, the memory of her own racing heartbeat-are enough to resurrect the threat response entirely. Her body remembers what her mind cannot fully access, and when these pieces arrive unbidden, they pull her back into a state of hypervigilance where every sound, every presence, every moment of unusual quiet feels pregnant with danger.

Margot came to therapy because her partner finally insisted. She is exhausted by her own vigilance, by the way she monitors every person who enters her classroom, by the way she still varies her route home even though the threat is long past. She is tired of being afraid, but more than that, she is afraid of what will happen if she stops being afraid-if she lets her guard down and the danger somehow returns. What she hopes for, though she barely dares to articulate it, is to feel like herself again, to trust that the world is not fundamentally dangerous, that she can be in a room without needing to know where every exit is.
